passage: "Ankita! Shoes! Now!" Papa's voice cracked like a whip. Ankita dropped her crayon and ran, and put her shoes on the wrong feet. "Good girl," said Papa. "See how fast she listens, Amma." "Look at her hands, Pankaj," said Dadi quietly. "They are shaking." "She is only being quick." "She is being careful. That is not the same." Ankita stood very still, watching Papa's face, waiting to see if she had done it right.

qa.q: What did Ankita do with her shoes?
qa.a: Ankita put her shoes on the wrong feet.

qa.q: What is Ankita feeling as she stands still watching Papa's face?
qa.a: Ankita feels anxious, waiting to learn whether she has avoided disapproval; the shaking hands and stillness show fear behind the quick obedience.

qa.q: What could Papa try the next time shoes are needed?
qa.a: Papa could call Ankita in an ordinary voice, walk over and help with the shoes, so listening comes from trust rather than fear.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Ankita's quick obedience?
qa.a: Dadi sees the shaking hands as carefulness born of worry, not good discipline, and says being quick and being careful are not the same.

grounding: A young child obeys quickly when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking like discipline while the inner state is anxiety.

passage: Observation note, KG2. When the room got noisy, the substitute teacher raised her voice: "Tidy up, now!" Lakshmi was the first up, packing blocks with wide eyes and a tight mouth, hardly looking at anyone. The other children finished slowly, chatting, and Manav kept building. At the end Lakshmi asked me quietly, "Am I in trouble?" I said no, and that the voice had been loud because the room was noisy. I plan to tell her parents at pickup that she seems to tidy up out of fear, and I will use a calm tone in class. — Karthik Sir

qa.q: Who was the first to pack away the blocks?
qa.a: Lakshmi was the first up, packing the blocks.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi ask "Am I in trouble?" after tidying up so quickly?
qa.a: Lakshmi feared disapproval; the wide eyes and tight mouth show anxiety behind the fast tidying.

qa.q: What did Karthik Sir plan to do about it?
qa.a: Karthik Sir planned to tell Lakshmi's parents at pickup that she seems to tidy up out of fear, and to use a calm tone in class.

qa.q: How might Manav have experienced the same loud voice, compared with Lakshmi?
qa.a: Manav kept building, so the voice seems to have carried less alarm for Manav; the same sound meant different things to different children.

grounding: A young child obeys quickly when an adult's voice turns sharp, and a teacher's note shows the anxiety behind the good behaviour.

passage:
Dadar platform roared with announcements. Their train was leaving in four minutes, and Minakshi mausi was dragging the big suitcase.
Zubin stopped to stare at a man selling balloons.
“ZUBIN! Hold my hand. NOW.”
He grabbed her dupatta at once, nearly tripping. On the train he sat perfectly straight, hands in his lap, while his cousins ran up the aisle.
“You're being so good,” said Mausaji.
Zubin whispered to Minakshi mausi, “Are you still angry at me?” She pulled him close. “No, jaan. I was scared of losing you.” Only then did he lean against her.

qa.q: How long before the train was leaving?
qa.a: The train was leaving in four minutes.

qa.q: Why did Zubin sit so straight on the train?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid his mausi was still angry, so he stayed very still to avoid more disapproval.

qa.q: What did Minakshi mausi do that helped Zubin?
qa.a: She explained she had been scared of losing him, not angry, and pulled him close, which let him relax.

qa.q: How might Mausaji have read Zubin's stillness?
qa.a: Mausaji saw it as good behaviour and praised him, without noticing the worry behind it.

grounding: Shows a young child obeying instantly when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking well-behaved while he is actually anxious.

passage:
At the art class in a Hyderabad apartment, Leela aunty clapped twice. “Crayons down. Sit straight!” Her voice had an edge today.
Noor dropped her crayon mid-flower and sat bolt upright, hands flat on the table. The two boys beside her kept giggling until aunty said, “Did you hear me?” Then they sat too.
“Look at Noor,” Leela aunty said. “Perfect.”
Noor didn't smile. She kept her eyes on the table until the class ended. In the lift, her mother asked, “Did you have fun?”
Noor said, “My tummy hurts.” At home she hid her half-finished flower under her bed.

qa.q: What did Leela aunty say when she clapped?
qa.a: She said, "Crayons down. Sit straight!"

qa.q: What was Noor feeling while she sat bolt upright?
qa.a: She felt anxious and tense; she didn't smile at the praise and later said her tummy hurt.

qa.q: How could Noor's mother gently find out more?
qa.a: She could sit with Noor calmly, ask about the flower and how aunty's voice felt, and let her know it's okay to feel scared.

qa.q: How might Leela aunty see Noor's behaviour?
qa.a: Leela aunty sees it as perfect discipline and praises it, not noticing the fear behind Noor's stillness.

grounding: Shows a young child who obeys at once when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking disciplined while inside she is anxious.

passage:
“Urmila. Shoes. Now,” said Devika chachi, sharper than usual. The school van was honking outside.
Urmila ran. She jammed her feet into her shoes without undoing the straps.
“Good girl,” said Chachaji, handing her the bag.
Her cousin Bunty was still eating his paratha. “I'm coming, Mamma.”
In the van, Urmila sat very still.
In the evening she found Chachaji watering the plants. “Is Chachi still cross?”
“Cross? No. Why?”
“Her voice went pointy.”
Chachaji knelt down. “She was rushing, that's all. You can ask her.”
Urmila shook her head and stayed near the plants until dinner.

qa.q: What was honking outside?
qa.a: The school van was honking outside.

qa.q: What does Urmila's question to Chachaji suggest she felt all day?
qa.a: She felt worried and scared that Chachi was still cross, because the sharp "pointy" voice stayed with her.

qa.q: What could Devika chachi do in the evening to help?
qa.a: She could tell Urmila herself that she wasn't cross, only rushing, and give her a hug, so Urmila doesn't carry the worry.

qa.q: Why might Bunty react differently to the sharp voice?
qa.a: Bunty took his time with his paratha, perhaps because he is used to his mother's rushing, while Urmila took the tone as danger.

grounding: Shows a young child who rushes to obey when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking good while inside she is anxious.

passage:
Note, KG-B, Tuesday.
Clean-up time was loud. Zubin and two others kept building. When our helper, Mrs Rao, snapped "Stop NOW," Mahima dropped her blocks at once and stood stiffly by the shelf, first to finish. Mrs Rao praised her, but Mahima did not smile. She kept glancing at Mrs Rao and twisting her pinafore.
Later she whispered to me, "Is Rao ma'am angry?" I sat beside her and said nobody was cross with her. I will suggest a calm clap-song signal for clean-up, and mention it to her parents at pickup.

qa.q: Who snapped "Stop NOW" at clean-up time?
qa.a: Mrs Rao, the helper, snapped "Stop NOW."

qa.q: What does Mahima's twisting of her pinafore suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mahima felt anxious and scared of disapproval, not proud, even though she looked like the best-behaved child.

qa.q: Why is a calm clap-song signal a better idea for clean-up?
qa.a: It gets the children moving without fear, so tidying comes from the routine rather than from worry about an angry voice.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Mahima's quick tidying?
qa.a: Mrs Rao probably sees it as good discipline and feels pleased, without noticing the worry behind it.

grounding: Shows a young child who obeys instantly when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking well-disciplined while actually anxious.
